content: The text provided is a dense and highly technical summary of various studies and systematic reviews related to physical activity (PA) and its association with health outcomes, including all-cause mortality, cardiovascular disease (CVD) mortality, CVD incidence, and other health-related outcomes. 1. Chastin et al. (2019): This study analyzed 12 prospective cohort studies with a total of 127,724 participants. The findings indicated a statistically significant reduction in all-cause mortality risk when comparing high levels of physical activity to low levels. However, there was notable inconsistency between studies, and the definitions of high and low activity levels varied across the included studies. Most of the research focused on adults over the age of 50. A pooled analysis of five studies demonstrated a significant reduction in all-cause mortality risk for individuals with the highest levels of physical activity compared to those with the lowest levels. 2. Dinu et al. (2019): This review included 11 prospective cohort studies with 231,259 participants. The studies evaluated the effects of active commuting (e.g., walking, cycling, or mixed modes) on health outcomes. The exposure levels were reported variably, such as minutes spent walking or cycling per day, dichotomized variables (yes/no), or metabolic equivalents (METs). Most studies used no active commuting as the reference category. Follow-up periods ranged from 4 to 25 years. The evidence showed a significant association between active commuting and reduced health risks, but there were serious concerns about bias, inconsistency, and indirectness in the comparisons. 3. Ekelund et al. (2019): This systematic review and meta-analysis included eight prospective cohort studies with 36,383 participants. All studies used accelerometers to measure physical activity and sedentary behavior. The exposure variables included total physical activity volume (counts per minute), time spent in specific intensity categories (e.g., sedentary, light, moderate-to-vigorous), and bouts of moderate-to-vigorous physical activity (MVPA). Higher levels of light-intensity physical activity, low light-intensity physical activity, high light-intensity physical activity, and MVPA were all significantly associated with reduced mortality risk. The maximal risk reductions were observed at approximately 375 minutes/day for light-intensity physical activity, 325 minutes/day for low light-intensity physical activity, 80 minutes/day for high light-intensity physical activity, and 24 minutes/day for MVPA. No further risk reductions were observed beyond these thresholds, except for low light-intensity physical activity, where additional reductions were noted. 4. Blond et al. (2019): This review included 48 prospective cohort studies, with five studies using accelerometers and the remainder relying on self-reported physical activity. The studies primarily focused on moderate-to-vigorous physical activity (MVPA) or leisure-time physical activity. The evidence demonstrated a dose-response relationship, with higher levels of physical activity associated with lower mortality risk. The absolute rate difference (ARD) was calculated as 16 fewer deaths per 10,000 person-years for individuals engaging in high levels of physical activity compared to those with very low levels. However, there was significant inconsistency between studies, and possible publication bias was noted. 5. Stamatakis et al. (2018): This pooled cohort analysis included 80,306 participants and evaluated adherence to both aerobic and strength-training physical activity guidelines. Adherence to both types of guidelines was associated with a significantly reduced risk of all-cause mortality. Participation in any strength-promoting exercise, including bodyweight exercises and gym-based activities, was also associated with reduced mortality risk. The analysis demonstrated no serious risk of bias, inconsistency, or indirectness, and the evidence quality was rated as good. 6. Amagasa et al. (2018): This review included four cohort studies with 17,133 participants aged 50 to 80 years. The studies used data from the National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey (NHANES) and compared replacing sedentary behavior with light physical activity (LPA). Three of the four studies found significant effects, particularly among women with low levels of MVPA. The evidence showed no serious risk of bias, inconsistency, or indirectness, and the findings were considered robust. 7. Dinu et al. (2019) – CVD Incidence: This review included five prospective cohort studies with 183,872 participants. The studies evaluated the effects of active commuting (cycling and/or walking) on cardiovascular disease (CVD) incidence. Exposure levels were reported variably, including minutes spent walking or cycling per day, dichotomized variables (yes/no), or METs. Most studies used no active commuting as the reference category. Follow-up periods ranged from 4 to 25 years. The evidence demonstrated a significant association between active commuting and reduced CVD incidence, but there were serious concerns about bias and indirectness. 8. Summary of Dose-Response Relationships: Across multiple studies, a dose-response relationship was observed between physical activity and health outcomes. Higher levels of physical activity, particularly MVPA, were consistently associated with reduced risks of all-cause mortality, CVD mortality, and CVD incidence. The benefits plateaued at specific thresholds, with no additional risk reductions observed beyond these levels for most activity types. 9.
